title: The table is the altar (Berakhot 55a)
hookLine: the Talmud says that now a person's table atones, through hospitality

lines: BREAD AND A DISH OF SALT.
cards: A plate of bread, a small dish of salt. At some Jewish tables, before the meal, someone says the blessing over the bread, breaks it, and touches each piece to the salt before passing it around.
It looks like a simple kitchen habit. Tradition ties it to a memory: in the Torah, the offerings brought to the altar were salted. "With all thine offerings thou shalt offer salt."
The altar is gone. The salt is still on the table. And the Talmud has a line about where the altar went.

teach.h: LINGER AT THE TABLE: A GUEST MAY COME.
teach.b: It's in tractate Berakhot, page fifty-five. The passage lists things that lengthen a person's days, and one is lingering long at your table. Why?
Because a poor person might come, and you'll be there to feed them.
Then two teachers, Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar, both say, in paraphrase: as long as the Temple stood, the altar atoned for Israel; now that it's gone, a person's table atones for them.

The rabbis anchor this in a verse from Ezekiel's vision of the future Temple. The verse begins by describing an altar of wood, and in the same breath calls it a table: "This is the table that is before the LORD."

teach.h: IT STARTS AS AN ALTAR, ENDS AS A TABLE.
teach.b: It starts as an altar and ends as a table.
The commentator Rashi explains how a table atones: through hospitality, by feeding guests and the hungry. So the rabbis took the altar, the center of the old worship, and set it down in the kitchen.
At Yavneh, words stood in for offerings. Here, a meal does. The house of God is gone, so every house gets a piece of its work.
The measure of a table isn't the food on it. It's who has a seat.
A meal shared with someone who needed one becomes, in the rabbis' language, a kind of offering, and some readers hear the salt on the bread as a small reminder of that.

how: In Jewish homes that keep the custom, the bread blessed at the start of a meal is touched to salt, a custom linked to the salted Temple offerings, and welcoming guests, hachnasat orchim, is counted a mitzvah.

games.q: the Temple is gone, and with it the altar that atoned. you're one of the rabbis. where do you say atonement can happen now?
o: nowhere, until the Temple is rebuilt.
at a person's table, through hospitality.
games.why: Rabbi Yochanan and Rabbi Elazar say a person's table now atones. Rashi explains: through feeding guests.

practice: Picture your own table: a dining table, a kitchen counter, the desk where you eat lunch.

Let a name come of someone who could have a seat there, someone lonely, someone new in town, a colleague eating alone, and picture the small details: what you'd serve, where they'd sit, the bread passed hand to hand.
If you pray, you can say a blessing you know before your next meal.
